headline: Nothing that runs at render time is free, and the shipped defaults now separate three ways: next-yak's css-prop fold ties hand-written `vanilla` at every composition depth on 2.66 kB of payload, the build-time atomic lanes trade their zero library slice for class-attribute bytes that cost them more react-dom time than their styling ever cost, and the libraries that name a class from its content pay for it twice, once on the server and again in the browser.

findings.title: Build-time compilation moves the cost into react-dom, it does not remove it
findings.prose: Every lane that resolves its classes during the build reports a library slice of roughly zero on the SSR profile, and the ordering among them is then decided by markup. On the Example `realistic-button` shown below, `stylex-layers` writes 5.55 kB of HTML with short hashed class names and spends 29.7 ms in react-dom, while `bamboo` writes 9.16 kB of readable atomic names and its react-dom slice reaches 79.0 ms, which is the entire 2.2× SSR gap between two lanes that do no styling work at all. The Example `tabs` shown below states it plainly: `bamboo`'s own package costs 0.012 ms of library slice and the case still costs it 3.08 ms, because 74.0 of its 84.6 ms of JS is react-dom escaping selector text out of the class attribute. Class naming is a performance decision, not a readability one.

findings.title: The css-prop fold is the only path that ignores composition depth
findings.prose: Down the composition ladder (the Examples `compose-1`, `compose-3` and `compose-6` shown below) `next-yak-css-9.7` concatenates the whole chain into one class on a plain element and renders at 0.522, 0.517 and 0.517 ms/1k on payloads of 2.67, 2.66 and 2.66 kB gzipped. Everything that merges classes instead pays per level: `bamboo` runs a `cx()` join at each one and climbs 0.553 to 1.13 ms/1k, `stylex-layers` runs `styleq` and climbs 0.530 to 1.36, `tailwind-merge` 0.540 to 2.49, `panda` re-resolves each level's object and reaches 3.47. next-yak's styled API rises only 0.448 to 0.698 ms/1k once its runtime collapses the `Yak → Yak` chain into a single component, but it keeps a residual wrapper wherever a styled component wraps another component, which is what costs it 1.77 against `vanilla`'s 0.838 ms/1k on the Example `tabs` shown below.

findings.title: A faster runtime is still a runtime, and it fails where the compiler cannot follow
findings.prose: `bamboo` and `panda` expose the same `css()` API, and on the Example `compose-1` shown below they ship a byte-identical source file. `bamboo` renders it at 0.553 ms/1k because its Vite plugin replaces the call with the resulting class string; `panda` renders it at 1.18 because `css()` resolves the object on every render, 0.518 ms of component self-time. The gap is modest while the object is static and widens with everything the compiler cannot precompute: 2.24 against 0.805 ms/1k at three composition levels, 3.47 against 1.13 at six, and 4.87 against 0.637 on the Example `dyn-translate` shown below, where `panda` mints an arbitrary-value class per element and 142 ms of its 157 ms JS window is spent inside its own package. `panda`'s precompiled `cva` recipe reaches 0.789 ms/1k on the Example `btn-variant` shown below against its own `css()` build's 1.57, so the fast path exists inside the library; what decides the number is whether the call site survives the build.

findings.title: Runtime hashing costs twice, once per render and again in the browser
findings.prose: The libraries that name a class from its content pay on the server and then repeat the work on the client. On the Example `product-grid` shown below, `@emotion/hash` and `@emotion/styled` take 171 ms of `emotion`'s 410 ms JS window and its interaction cost reaches 52.6 ms against the static-class lanes' 8.3-10.5. The browser side is worse: `goober` and `styled-components` inject their sheet during hydration, so the Example `tabs` shown below records 2.13-2.23 ms of style recalculation, a 3.5-3.7 ms layout pass and 18 presented frames inside a span where every extracted lane shows zero and one. On the naive dynamic Example `dyn-translate` shown below `goober` mints a thousand distinct classes and its cold mount reaches 1,320 ms against a 65.7 ms floor. Extraction is the whole cure and it is paid for during the build instead, `panda` and `stylex-layers` cold-building in 305-408 ms and `bamboo` in 1,990 ms against 72-129 ms for everything else.

findings.title: Dynamic values are a compiler feature in next-yak and a discipline everywhere else
findings.prose: next-yak compiles a dynamic value into a static class plus a CSS custom property automatically, so its figures are the same on the naive Example `dyn-translate` and the hand-tuned Example `dyn-fair` shown below, 0.596 against 0.617 ms/1k: there was nothing to change. Everyone else sits in one case or the other depending on developer discipline. `goober` renders at 5.98 ms/1k and mounts in 1,320 ms with the obvious spelling, then at 1.06 ms/1k and 86.1 ms once a person splits the static class from the inline style by hand; `styled-components` moves 4.51 to 1.35 ms/1k and sheds 16.4 kB of payload. That split is a build-time optimization performed manually, per component, on every dynamic value, for the life of the codebase, and the naive case is what the same code costs the day nobody performs it. `bamboo` takes a third route and refuses to compile a runtime value inside `css()` at all, so its two files are the same code and its two figures are the same figure.

findings.title: Payload separates the extracted lanes from everything else on a real page
findings.prose: On the Example `product-grid` shown below, a page of 400 tiles, `next-yak-css-9.7` ships 7.14 kB gzipped and hand-written `vanilla` 7.79, while atomic and utility naming doubles or triples that: `stylex-layers` 13.0 kB, `bamboo` 17.3, `panda` 22.2, `cnfast` 27.7. The mechanism is that atomic systems write every rule twice, once into the sheet and once into the class attribute of every element that uses it, so payload grows with element count rather than with rule count. The Example `tabs` shown below is the extreme: identical CSS costs 2.37 kB through the css-prop fold and 16.1 kB through `panda`, 10.1 kB of it markup, and the fold holds its figure at every composition depth.

libraryHints.hint: Both APIs stay flat under depth; the open lever is folding through `styled(Component)` seams, worth 1.77 → 0.858 ms/1k on `tabs`.
Zero styling runtime, but readable class names land in the markup: `tabs` spends 74.0 of 84.6 ms in react-dom escaping them. Offer hashed names in production builds.

`css()` still resolves per render wherever a call site is not hoisted; fold static call sites to their class string at build time, as `cva` already effectively does (0.789 vs 1.57 ms/1k on `btn-variant`).
Nothing on the render path for flat JSX; `styleq`'s per-element merge is the remaining cost, climbing 0.530 to 1.36 ms/1k from one composition level to six.

`generateAndInjectStyles` re-hashes and injects per render (4.55 ms of the `realistic-button` slice); hash the static rule once and ride dynamic values on a variable, as its own `.attrs` path already does.
`murmur2` re-hashes the whole serialized string every render (100 of 219 ms of JS on `realistic-button`); memoize the hash on the serialized-string identity for static components.
The compile-and-hash runs per render and injects a class per distinct value (`dyn-translate` mounts in 1,320 ms); key the cache on the tagged-template identity, not the interpolated result.

The merge rebuilds and re-looks-up the joined-class key every render (1.69 ms of the `realistic-button` slice, six times over at depth 6); cache on argument identity, or hoist a fully static merge to a constant.
Near-free on repeated class lists; only high-cardinality dynamic classes cost, through the cache miss. Split the invariant prefix from the volatile token so the prefix stays a hit.
